text: A man keeps a lighthouse on Lake Michigan and does not cash his paychecks. David Charleston's only appointment is the inspector's monthly visit; the rest of his company drowned in the 1800s, aboard a packet ship that went down near his rock, and he holds conversations with them anyway. Once he was a journalist with a name. Through the 1930s he told his editors, and then anyone else who would sit still, that fascism meant war, and was heard by almost nobody. The drowned carry unfinished business of their own, a woman who wanted a life not arranged by men, a doctor expelled for his methods, so the lighthouse fills with people who spoke too early. Released in 1944, with the argument long since settled by events, it plays less as fantasy than as a hearing granted late.

Zara sings in a bar, drinks past the point of pleasure, and cannot say whether she is somebody else's missing wife. A man called Tony turns up at the novelist's estate where she is living and tells her she is Maria, lost to the war, and she goes with him: to Italy, to Bruno, an army officer coaxing a past out of a woman with no way to confirm it. Seventy minutes is a short span for a case this unstable, and the film spends it well, because every tenderness offered to her doubles as a test she might fail. The 1932 machinery is frank, with its amnesia, its estate, its rival claimant produced to settle matters. Underneath sits something harder: a woman assembled to specification by men who have already agreed on what she ought to be, including the one who says he loves her.

A bishop is expected for dinner, and the wrong guests get there first. The household belongs to a railway brakeman and his wife, the incident coming out of the lives of Neal and Carolyn Cassady, and for twenty-six minutes the rooms fill with friends who have no intention of behaving in front of clergy. Robert Frank and Alfred Leslie shot it. Jack Kerouac took the third act of his play Beat Generation, cut it down, and then talked over the finished images, improvising every voice in the room, so that one man ends up performing an entire party. That is the whole method, and it changes what is on screen: bodies moving without their own words, dubbed by a friend inventing them on the spot, a wrecked dinner turned into a home movie with a novelist heckling from the dark.

The low-rider is not decoration here; it is the younger brother's entire argument about how to live. Raymond Avila has worked his way clear of the gang and has something like a future to name. Chuco has not, and the film declines to turn that into a moral gap between them, because the bond holds regardless. What tightens the hundred minutes is the schedule nobody controls: a rival crew makes a move, and everyone except Raymond expects Chuco to answer it. Michael Pressman lets the ordinary run long first, the work, the household, the boulevard on a warm evening, so that when the trouble lands it lands on people rather than positions. The National Film Registry keeps it. The interest is the arithmetic inside a family whose members love one another and cannot agree on what a week should contain.

Two sisters, a policeman courting one of them, and a ring that sells women: the parts are melodrama, and the year is 1913. Eighty-eight minutes of it, which asked a great deal of an audience then, and the length goes into procedure rather than sensation, into watching and following and gathering enough to hand to someone with a badge. The nerve of the thing is its insistence that a trade like this runs on capital and respectability, not on a brute in a doorway. Its heroine does the finding out herself, which the plot treats as unremarkable. The National Film Registry preserves it. What comes through now is the mixture in the tone, alarm braided with fascination, a moral warning that cannot look away from the mechanics of what it is warning about.

The plow is the villain of this documentary, and not as a figure of speech. Pare Lorentz had twenty-five minutes in 1936 to account for what farming without limit did to the Great Plains of the United States and Canada: grass broken up, soil left holding nothing, and then the wind that had always been there doing the rest. Documentary had no settled manners at that date, and the film uses the freedom, pitching its voice somewhere between a report and a sermon and giving the machinery more presence than any individual farmer. The result argues rather than observes. It also refuses the comfort of calling the Dust Bowl weather, which is the harder position, and the reason the National Film Registry holds on to a short that could have been left behind as a pamphlet with pictures.

The sums do not come out, and rearranging the ledger will not make them. William Marble, a bank clerk with bills he cannot meet, asks his wealthy nephew for a loan, is refused, and settles on murder, a decision the film hands over early so that the remaining hour is not a question of who but of what money does to a frightened man once he has it. Eighty-one minutes, 1932, and most of them domestic: callers to be managed, questions from the household, rooms too small to hold a secret this size. Lothar Mendes lets the crime work like damp in the walls. The National Board of Review placed it among the year's ten best, and the reason is not the killing at all but the long stretch after it, a man guarding a fortune from the family he took it for.

The Golden Globes once handed a prize called Best Film Promoting International Understanding to a comedy about a Jewish refugee and the antisemite at the wheel. Paris is falling. Jacobowsky needs to be somewhere else, Colonel Prokoszny has a car, contempt and no better plan, and what the two arrive at is not friendship but a route. Then Suzanne, the Colonel's intended, joins them and finds Jacobowsky good company, which does nothing to improve the atmosphere in the front seat. The film runs 109 minutes and never lets the dislike dissolve, which is exactly why the comedy holds: the pursuit behind them is real, the prejudice inside the car is real, and neither one cancels the other. Jacobowsky is right about almost everything, and the Colonel is determined not to notice.

Tae-joo gets his promotion the stupid way, by happening to be standing there when the boss's life needs saving. From that accident the film builds a three-cornered fight: a gangster on the way up, a prosecutor named Dong-pal whose temper is no better than that of the men he pursues, and Jo-pil, training for revenge with the discipline of someone who has nothing else on. Song Neung-han shoots the violence fast and lets the talking run long, and the talking is where the comedy sits, since everyone in this world knows everyone and rank is kept in a ledger of remembered humiliations. The Korean Film Archive's list of a hundred films carries it. What keeps 108 minutes alive is the distance between how these men describe themselves and the seating order everybody else can see.

Eight minutes, and each shot lasts about a second, which is roughly the time recognition takes. Chuck Workman cut close to a century of American movies together at that rhythm, Citizen Kane and Some Like It Hot, Star Wars and E.T., so the film arrives faster than thought and slower than forgetting. What it measures is not film history but what an audience has kept. Fragments show up with their emotional charge intact and nowhere to spend it, which produces the trance the piece is after: feeling detached from any story that would justify it. It took the Academy Award for Best Live Action Short Film, a category it fits only by default, being neither acted nor, in the ordinary sense, staged. The material already existed. The work lies entirely in the order.

Quasi is a duck, Anita is a duck, Rollo is a robot, and the amusement park is stranger than any of them. Sally Cruikshank hand-drew ten minutes of it in 1975, and the plot is a plot only on a technicality: Quasi behaves badly and his companions run out of patience with him. Everything else is invention for its own sake, rides that appear to run on principles other than physics, background business that rewards a second pass, a general willingness to follow a shape wherever it wants to go. None of it is aimed at children, exactly, though nothing is hidden from them either. The National Film Registry took it in, an odd destination for a cartoon so uninterested in being wholesome, and a fair one for a short that turns a day out with friends into a small, slightly hostile dream.

The funeral is over before the film begins, and everything after it is testimony. Tom Garner started as a track walker, covering rails on foot, and ended at the head of the railroad; the picture refuses to lay that rise out in order, cutting between the young man and the executive until cost and achievement keep occupying the same minute. Seventy-six minutes, no slack. What Garner loses is his family, and he registers the loss long after the fact, which the structure makes visible in a way straight chronology could not, since the bill is presented to the audience well before it reaches him. Made in 1933, when a story about a self-made man carried its own sting, and built on a question he never quite asks himself: who was paying, all that time, for the climb.

A mother starts reading her own son's face for evidence. The suspicion never leaves the house, which is what makes the film hard to shake off rather than merely dated, and the accused is a grown child who comes home, is polite, and gives her nothing to hold. Leo McCarey directs 122 minutes of it in 1952 without a trace of a wink, and the tenderness and the accusation plainly issue from the same place in him. Balance is not attempted. What still works is the mother's position: asked to weigh her feeling for her son against a fear the era has handed her, she begins watching for signs, and once the watching starts everything qualifies as one. Belief and doubt run on the same machinery here. Both are conducted in a living room.

A photograph is laid on a hot plate and the camera stays with it while it curls, darkens and goes. Then another. Hollis Frampton supplies both the pictures and the first-person account of them; Michael Snow reads that account aloud as if he were Frampton, so the voice claiming these memories is not the one that formed them. Thirty-six minutes of the arrangement. The effect is peculiar and exact: an image is described in language at the moment it is being destroyed as an object, and the description is what survives. A career's early evidence goes up one sheet at a time, narrated in a borrowed voice, dry as an inventory. The National Film Registry keeps it. The humour in that dryness is real, and so is the small panic of reaching for a picture already gone.
